speaker: David Baker
title: Nobel Laureate David Baker on Using AI for Science to Solve Humanity's Biggest Problems
question: In AI for biology, why is it risky to extrapolate the rapid success of protein structure prediction to higher levels of biological complexity?
guest: With protein structure prediction and protein design, there might be a tendency to over-extrapolate from it. The key thing is that the first protein structures were solved in the 1960s, and since then tens of thousands of graduate students and postdocs spent their careers solving them—each protein structure was a PhD. Another large group of scientists curated a very precise, accurate database, with global investment probably in the tens of billions of dollars over fifty or sixty years. It's like fossil fuel: we burned fast because all this work was done before. As we move up the biological complexity hierarchy, we don't have datasets of that category. Many groups are developing internal datasets, but it's not clear any single entity, even one very deeply funded, can collect enough data, and it's not even clear what data to collect. With things like ChatGPT, you train on a boring task like next-word prediction and get emergent reasoning, which has driven lots of money into collecting data hoping emergent properties appear. With text there's just so much of it. So I think people may be over-extrapolating from protein structure prediction.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Protein structure prediction was an unusually favorable problem, and the conditions that made it tractable mostly disappear at higher levels of biology.

Structure prediction had a well-defined question (sequence to 3D structure) with a largely deterministic physical answer. It also had decades of standardized, high-quality data in the Protein Data Bank, plus vast sequence databases whose evolutionary covariation carries strong structural signal. And it had a clear objective benchmark in CASP, so progress was measurable.

Cells, tissues and organisms offer none of this cleanly. Their behavior is context-dependent, dynamic, stochastic and emergent across many interacting scales, so there is often no single "ground truth" to predict. The data are sparser relative to the complexity, noisier, shaped by batch effects, and mostly observational snapshots rather than causal perturbations. Benchmarks are weak or contested; for example, deep-learning models for predicting gene-perturbation effects have often failed to beat simple linear baselines.

Even within structure, AlphaFold predicts static shapes more reliably than dynamics, disordered regions, or the effects of mutations, and accurate structures have not automatically translated into understanding function or producing successful drugs. The success therefore reflects a rare match of problem, data and metric, not evidence that biology in general will yield as quickly.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Protein structure prediction succeeded rapidly because it addressed a uniquely bounded problem: mapping an amino acid sequence to a largely static, low-energy 3D conformation. Models like AlphaFold benefited from fifty years of standardized, atomic-resolution structures in the Protein Data Bank, rich evolutionary co-variation across billions of sequences, and clear ground-truth benchmarks like CASP.

Higher levels of biological organization, such as cells, tissues, and organisms, lack these foundations. No equivalent of the PDB exists for cellular dynamics; instead, experimental datasets are fragmented across modalities, noisy, sparse, and confounded by batch effects, leaving most molecular interactions unobserved in time and space. Furthermore, living systems are open, non-equilibrium networks governed by stochasticity, nonlinear feedback, spatial compartmentalization, and environmental context rather than sequence alone. Predicting cellular phenotypes or clinical outcomes therefore shifts the challenge from structural pattern recognition to causal reasoning across vast combinatorial perturbations, where out-of-distribution generalization remains difficult and wet-lab validation is slow and costly.

noweb.answer: Extrapolating the success of protein structure prediction to cells, tissues, or whole organisms is risky because protein folding possessed uniquely favorable conditions that vanish at higher biological scales. Models like AlphaFold relied on decades of standardized, atomic-resolution structures in the Protein Data Bank paired with massive evolutionary sequence databases whose co-variation patterns directly encode 3D contact constraints. Moreover, mapping a single amino acid sequence to a static, low-energy conformation is a tightly bounded problem with limited dependence on external context. Higher-level biology lacks both this clean problem formulation and any equivalent gold-standard dataset. Cellular and physiological phenotypes emerge from dynamic, non-equilibrium networks spanning genes, proteins, metabolites, cell-cell signaling, and environmental exposures, where spatial context, history, and stochasticity dominate. Experimental measurements at these scales remain sparse, noisy, protocol-dependent, and largely observational, offering isolated snapshots rather than the interventional time-series data required to learn causal mechanisms. Without unified multi-scale perturbation datasets and strong evolutionary invariants, scaling compute and model architecture alone cannot replicate the protein-folding breakthrough.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Protein structure prediction worked unusually well, and the conditions behind that success mostly don't carry over to cells, tissues or organisms. AlphaFold built on decades of structures in the Protein Data Bank, which are standardized, high-quality, experimentally validated and openly shared. It also had a well-defined target, since a sequence largely determines a stable fold. And it had an objective benchmark, CASP, run with blind tests. The physics also limits the problem: evolution has produced only a finite set of folds, and coevolution signals in sequence alignments carry strong structural information.

Higher levels of biology lack most of these things. Cellular and organismal behavior is dynamic and depends on context. It is shaped by environment, cell state, stochastic noise, and interactions across many scales. Data for these levels are sparse, noisy and affected by batch effects. They are often observational rather than causal, and they're rarely collected in standardized form. Often there is no agreed "ground truth" or clear objective to predict, which makes rigorous benchmarking hard. Combinatorial complexity explodes, and mechanisms are often emergent, not encoded in one sequence. So early successes like "virtual cell" models may simply mean the models learned correlations, and treating them as AlphaFold-like breakthroughs risks overhype, misplaced investment, and false confidence in their predictions.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Protein structure prediction succeeded rapidly because it sat in an unusually favorable regime for machine learning: a well-defined, largely static mapping from sequence to 3D shape, supported by decades of standardized, high-resolution structural data in the Protein Data Bank and vast evolutionary sequence databases. Higher levels of biological complexity—cellular signaling, gene regulation, tissue physiology, and organismal health—lack these advantages. They are dynamic, non-equilibrium systems governed by emergent properties, nonlinear feedback loops, and strong dependence on spatial, temporal, and environmental context. Experimental data at these scales is also noisier, less standardized, and far sparser relative to the vast combinatorial space of biological states and perturbations. Moreover, validation becomes dramatically harder: comparing a predicted fold to a crystal structure is clear-cut, whereas testing whether an intervention safely alters a disease pathway requires causal understanding and slow, costly experiments. Extrapolating from folding to higher scales therefore underestimates both data bottlenecks and systemic complexity.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Protein structure prediction had unusually favorable conditions for AI. Researchers had decades of experimentally determined structures, vast sequence databases, and a clear benchmark for whether a predicted structure matched an observed one. A protein sequence can strongly constrain its fold, so models had a stable relationship to learn.

At the level of cells, tissues, and organisms, the same genes and proteins can produce different outcomes depending on cell state, environmental conditions, and what happened earlier. Measurements often cover only a subset of the relevant variables, and experiments that test what happens after a perturbation are much sparser than snapshots. A model can therefore predict familiar observations accurately and still fail when asked what a new intervention will do. Rapid progress on protein folding tells us what AI can achieve when the data and the target are well matched. The pace of progress at higher levels depends on how well we can measure, perturb, and validate those systems.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Protein structure prediction made rapid progress on a relatively well-defined task: given an amino acid sequence, predict a likely three-dimensional structure. Large collections of experimentally measured structures gave researchers a way to train models and check their predictions.

At higher levels of complexity, even an accurate structure leaves crucial questions open. Which molecules a protein interacts with, when it is active, and what happens if its activity changes can all depend on the cell type and its environment. For example, two cell types can respond differently to the same drug because one can compensate through an alternative pathway. Predicting that response requires understanding how the system changes over time, and experiments cover only a fraction of the relevant conditions. Success at predicting molecular shape therefore gives little basis for assuming equally rapid progress in predicting cellular behavior or disease.
